title: Damien of Molokai
hookLine: a priest goes to a settlement for people with leprosy, and one day begins his sermon, we lepers

cards: Boats struggle to land at this beach. Cliffs stand behind it like a wall, the sea in front is rough, and people are put ashore however the crew can manage. Once they're here, they don't leave.

This strip of the Hawaiian island of Molokai is where the kingdom sent people with leprosy, now called Hansen's disease, to keep them away from everyone else. Families said goodbye on the dock in Honolulu.
A young Belgian priest, Father Damien, offers to go. He builds houses, digs graves, dresses sores, plays with the children. And one Sunday, tradition says, he changes a single word.

teach.b: Damien had preached to the settlement the way an outsider would. You. Your suffering.
Your hope. Then he noticed the signs of the disease on his own body. He had caught it.
The story told about the next Sunday is short: he began his sermon with two words, we lepers. Not you. We.

That word is the whole lesson. Plenty of people helped the settlement from a safe distance. Damien was now inside it, with no way back out, and the people he served, the story goes, heard the difference.

Behind it is a scene in Mark. A man with leprosy kneels before Jesus: if you want to, you can make me clean. In the King James Bible: "And Jesus, moved with compassion, put forth his hand, and touched him."
The law of the time kept people with that disease apart, and the story stops to say Jesus reached out a hand before he said a word.

teach.h: HE CATCHES IT, AND SAYS WE.
teach.b: Hebrews says of Jesus and the people he came for: "he is not ashamed to call them brethren."
Some Christians read Damien's life as that sentence, lived out on a beach. He kept working after the diagnosis, and the disease took his life on Molokai.

The Catholic Church names him a saint, and Christians of other churches honor him too. One honest note. Some of the people sent to Molokai would rather not be called lepers at all; it names a person by a disease.

teach.h: NOT ASHAMED TO CALL THEM BRETHREN.
teach.b: Damien could say the word only because he'd become one of them. The lesson isn't the label. It's the we.

how: Catholics keep Saint Damien's feast and pray for people with Hansen's disease and for those who care for them, and Christians of other churches also tell his story when they talk about serving people pushed to the margins.

games.q: you're Father Damien. you've served the settlement for years, and now you see the signs of the disease on your own skin. what do you say next Sunday?
o: nothing. keep preaching to you, as always.
begin the sermon with we lepers.
announce that you'll be going home.
games.why: tradition says he began, we lepers. the people heard that he was no longer a visitor.

practice: Name, quietly, a group people talk about as they: the unhoused man on the corner, the kid nobody sits with, people with an illness others fear. Then try the word we instead: we who get sick, we who get left out, we who need a hand.
If you pray, pray for them as we; if you don't, just let the we sit there.

wordCard.voice: Damien. The priest who went to live with people sent away for leprosy on Molokai, caught the disease himself, and began preaching, we lepers.

orig.note: Greek: the word for a man with leprosy in Mark 1:40, the man Jesus touched.

carryVoice: Your line: we lepers. Not you, but we, said from the inside. See you tomorrow.
